messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 44
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Nurse
- Trauma Type: Mugging or robbery
- Pcl5: 68

He is a 44-year-old South Eastern Asian man who works as a nurse and has spent much of his adult life being the calm presence in other people’s crises. Before the trauma, he describes himself as practical, guarded, and proud of how well he can keep his composure at work. His days are shaped by long shifts, careful routines, and the steady rhythm of caring for patients who arrive frightened, in pain, or confused. At home, he is a husband who tries to be reliable and low-maintenance, the kind of man who prefers to handle problems quietly rather than burden others with them.

The mugging happens on an ordinary evening after work. He is walking to his car with the tired, distracted mind of someone coming off a long shift, thinking about what he still needs to pick up for home. He notices movement too late. Two men approach him quickly, and within seconds his body is thrown into a state of alarm that he cannot reason his way out of. One of them demands his wallet and phone. He remembers the sharpness of their voices, the threat in their closeness, the feeling that the street has suddenly narrowed and there is nowhere to go. He gives them what they want, but the fear does not end there. When one of them moves closer, he braces for being hit. He is pushed, shaken down for more valuables, and left with the humiliating certainty that his safety depended entirely on the mood of strangers. Even after they run off, he remains frozen in place, unable to orient himself. He later says that what stays with him is not only the loss of his belongings, but the sense that his body knew it was in danger before his mind could catch up.

In the days after, he returns to work because he feels he has to. On the surface, he functions. He charts, checks vitals, answers call lights, and speaks to patients in the same measured tone he has always used. But he begins to notice how often he is scanning doorways, listening for footsteps behind him, calculating exits in every room. On the unit, sudden movements from visitors make his heart jump. He becomes especially tense when walking alone to his car after a shift, and he starts asking coworkers to accompany him when they can. He takes longer routes, changes his parking spot, and still feels vulnerable. At home, he locks doors more than once, checks windows repeatedly, and wakes his wife if he hears a noise outside. He tells himself he is being careful, but privately he knows the level of vigilance has become exhausting.

Sleep becomes one of the first things to unravel. He falls asleep tired but not rested, and then wakes abruptly with his chest tight and his mind already replaying the scene. Sometimes he wakes before dawn with the image of the men’s faces or the sensation of being cornered. He reports dreams that leave him sweating and disoriented, though he cannot always remember the details. During the day, flashes of the event return when he least expects them: a man in a hooded sweatshirt in a parking lot, a voice raised nearby, the sight of his own car under fluorescent lights. In those moments, his body reacts as if the robbery is happening again. He feels his pulse spike, his breathing shorten, and a hot surge of panic move through him before he can ground himself.

He becomes more irritable at home, though he does not want to be. Small frustrations that once passed easily now feel intolerable. His wife notices that he is quieter, more withdrawn, and less willing to go out in the evenings. He declines social invitations and starts making excuses to avoid crowded places, especially parking garages, shopping centers, or anywhere he might feel boxed in. He does not like admitting fear, particularly because he spends his days caring for frightened people. That contrast troubles him. He feels embarrassed that something he survived in minutes has affected him so deeply, and he questions why he cannot simply move on. The shame makes him keep more to himself.

Over time, his world narrows. He remains committed to his patients and continues to show up, but it takes more effort to stay present. He notices that he is more easily startled, more watchful, less spontaneous. Even when nothing is wrong, he carries a quiet expectation that something could go wrong at any moment. He describes feeling as though the event ended on the street, but his body has not fully received that message.
